newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China's rural women more vulnerable to suicide.
newsitem.headline: China's rural women more vulnerable to suicide.

text.p: Young women in rural China are most vulnerable to suicide, an international charity group said on Tuesday.

Befrienders International, a charity recognised for its work in the prevention of suicides, has begun pushing into China, a country which already has the second highest suicide rate in the world, behind Hungary.

"In China, the suicide rate is highest among rural women aged between 15 and 39 years, and who appear to be having the most difficulty adjusting to rapid socio-economic change," regional director, Ewan Simpson, told a news conference in the British colony of Hong Kong.
"These women are often under tremendous pressure in caring for their family from a young age, and live a fairly lonely existence in a harsh matriarchal society," he said.
Ninety-three percent of those who committed suicide in China over the past four years were rural dwellers, a growing proportion of them young women, he said.

Recent studies have shown that the pattern of suicides in China, where women are killing themselves at double the rate of men, is opposite to that of "Westernised" Chinese societies and developed countries in which mainly male city dwellers take their own lives.
Simpson said his group was also concentrating efforts on Hong Kong where a record 776 people killed themselves last year -- one of the highest suicide rates in the region.
The trend was alarmingly prevalent among Hong Kong's youth, with children as young as five known to have killed themselves because of problems ranging from homework to family arguments.
In a city where most of the population live in densely- packed high-rise buildings, the most common methods of suicide were jumping from heights, and hanging.

"Hong Kong now represents the highest urban density in the world marked by problems of over-crowding, lack of sufficient housing, and a weakening of family support and kinship as relationships in this metropolitan city have become more and more impersonal," Simpson said.
The group's research showed the most vulnerable groups in Hong Kong were men in the 25 to 29 age group.
